text:
“I’m currently a corporal and due to be discharged next June. I already owe around 20 million won ($15,000) to banks, savings banks and other lenders,” reads a November post by a Gyeonggi Province-based soldier on an online platform matching borrowers with private moneylenders. “Is there anywhere I could get my hands on 5 million won?”
Such appeals are becoming harder to ignore as more young servicemen in Korea turn to high-interest lenders to finance online gambling and cryptocurrency investments. The problem has grown serious enough for financial authorities to move to curb a source of credit that many soldiers have come to rely on: personal loans from private lenders.
The scale of the shift is striking. Loans extended to active-duty servicemen by the country’s 30 largest registered loan companies totaled 24.2 billion won in 2025, nearly 69 times the 350 million won recorded in 2022, according to the Financial Services Commission.
Authorities point to the growing accessibility of online betting and speculative investments as a key factor. Soldiers have been able to use smartphones freely after duty hours since 2020, giving some of them easier access to gambling sites from their barracks.
At the same time, military pay has risen considerably: Monthly compensation for sergeants, for instance, has more than doubled from 676,100 won in 2022 to 1.5 million won this year.
The extent of the problem is difficult to measure, but Army figures offer one indication. Military police booked 1,721 servicemen on suspicion of online gambling between 2021 and 2025. That may be a small share of the Army’s more than 320,000 personnel, but soldiers note that online betting is far more widespread among their peers than the official figures suggest.
The consequences are also showing up in applications for debt relief. The number of active-duty personnel seeking help from the Credit Counseling & Recovery Service remained in the 400s annually from 2019 to 2021, then jumped to 753 in 2022 and 1,015 the following year. Another 322 had applied by April this year, putting the annual total on course to approach 1,000.
Their financial burdens have grown heavier, too. Average debt among servicemen seeking restructuring rose from 34.01 million won in 2019 to more than 50 million won in 2022, reaching 58.63 million won as of April this year.
“Debt among servicemen should be understood as part of the broader problem of mounting debt among young people, rather than as an issue unique to the military,” said Yang Jun-seok, a professor of economics at the Catholic University of Korea. “Young people are increasingly exposed to financial risks as they take a more active interest in high-risk assets such as cryptocurrencies.”
Mainstream lenders like banks and savings banks generally do not offer unsecured personal loans to active-duty soldiers, who lack the conventional income documents required to qualify. Private lenders, by contrast, have extended credit to soldiers by accepting copies of military pay account statements as proof of income.
In response, the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) has agreed with the Korea Consumer Loan Finance Association to add a provision to the industry’s standard operating guidelines by year-end that would bar private lenders from offering general-purpose personal loans to active-duty servicemen.
The FSS also plans to step up financial education in the military, expanding one-on-one counseling and programs warning of the risks of online gambling and leveraged investments.
